title: Explain how Peterson's Solution uses the flag[] array and the turn variable together to satisfy Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting for two processes.
chunks:
Mutual Exclusion: P0 sets flag[0]=true and turn=1. It only enters if flag[1]==false OR turn==0. If P1 is inside, flag[1] is true and turn would be 1, so P0 is blocked. They cannot both enter.

Progress: If P1 doesn't want to enter, flag[1] is false, so P0 can enter immediately without being indefinitely postponed.

Bounded Waiting: When P0 exits, it sets flag[0]=false. This immediately allows P1 (who might be waiting) to enter. P0 cannot re-enter and starve P1 because P0 will set turn=1 upon re-requesting, forcing itself to wait for P1.

title: Explain the Producer–Consumer problem using Shared Memory, describing the buffer and the shared variables involved (counter, in, out) and the role of the producer and consumer.
chunks:
The Producer-Consumer problem occurs when two processes share a fixed-size buffer. The Producer generates data and puts it into the buffer; the Consumer takes data out.

Shared Variables:

buffer[BUFFER_SIZE]: A circular array.

in: The index where the next item will be inserted.

out: The index where the next item will be consumed.

counter: Tracks the total number of items currently in the buffer.

The Role / Rules: The Producer must not try to insert data when counter == BUFFER_SIZE (buffer is full). The Consumer must not try to remove data when counter == 0 (buffer is empty). Synchronization is required to ensure counter++ and counter-- do not create a race condition.

title: Explain Peterson's Solution in detail, including its shared variables, working, and how it satisfies the requirements of the Critical-Section Problem.
chunks:
Peterson's Solution is a software-based synchronization algorithm for two processes (P0 and P1).

Shared Variables:

boolean flag[2] = {false, false}; (Indicates if a process wants to enter).

int turn; (Indicates whose turn it actually is).

Working (Code for P0):

flag[0] = true;

turn = 1; // Be polite, offer turn to P1

while (flag[1] == true && turn == 1); // Wait if P1 wants it AND it's P1's turn

...Critical Section...

flag[0] = false; // Exit

Requirements Satisfied: It guarantees Mutual exclusion (only one process can have turn == its_id), Progress (a process only waits if the other actively wants to enter), and Bounded waiting (the turn variable acts as a strict alternator, preventing starvation).

title: Explain Semaphores in detail — their two fundamental operations (wait and signal), their types (counting and binary), and their disadvantages (busy waiting and possibility of deadlock).
chunks:
A Semaphore (S) is an integer variable accessed only through two atomic operations:

wait(S): while(S <= 0); S--; (Waits until S > 0, then decrements it).

signal(S): S++; (Increments S).

Types:

Binary (Mutex): S is 0 or 1. Used for mutual exclusion.

Counting: S can be any integer. Used to manage a pool of identical resources.

Disadvantages:

Busy Waiting (Spinlock): Standard semaphores waste CPU cycles looping endlessly in wait() if the lock isn't free.

Deadlock: If two processes hold one semaphore each and wait for the other's, they freeze forever.

title: Explain the three requirements of a solution to the Critical-Section Problem — Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting — describing the significance of each with examples.
chunks:
Mutual Exclusion: Absolute prevention of simultaneous access. Significance: If P1 is writing to a bank balance variable, P2 cannot read or write to it, preventing corrupted math.

Progress: If the critical section is empty, processes that wish to enter cannot be blocked forever by processes executing in their remainder sections. Significance: Ensures the system doesn't freeze just because nobody is currently using the shared resource.

Bounded Waiting: A bound must exist on the number of times other processes are allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has made a request to enter its own. Significance: Prevents starvation. P1 shouldn't have to wait forever while P2 rapidly enters and exits 100 times.

title: A shared buffer of size 5 is used by a Producer and a Consumer, and currently holds 3 items. Using the semaphores mutex = 1, empty, and full as described in class, determine the current values of empty and full, and explain step-by-step (in terms of wait/signal calls) what happens when the Producer inserts one more item into the buffer.
chunks:
Since buffer size = 5 and it holds 3 items: full = 3, and empty = 2.

Step-by-Step Insertion:

Producer executes wait(empty). empty decrements from 2 to 1. (Checks if there is space).

Producer executes wait(mutex). mutex becomes 0. (Locks the buffer for exclusive access).

Producer inserts the new item into the buffer.

Producer executes signal(mutex). mutex becomes 1. (Unlocks the buffer).

Producer executes signal(full). full increments from 3 to 4. (Notifies the Consumer that a new item is available).

title: A hospital's patient database is read by many doctors at the same time but updated by only one nurse at a time; while a nurse is updating a record, no doctor should be able to read stale or partial data. Model this as the Readers–Writers problem: identify the semaphores/variables required (mutex, wrt, readcount), and explain the entry-section and exit-section logic for a reader process.
chunks:
Variables Required:

mutex (initialized to 1): Protects the readcount variable.

wrt (initialized to 1): The main lock for the database, preventing Writers from entering if anyone is inside.

readcount (initialized to 0): Number of active doctors (readers).

Reader Logic (Doctors):

Entry Section: The doctor executes wait(mutex) to safely increment readcount. If this doctor is the very first reader (readcount == 1), they execute wait(wrt) to lock out all nurses (writers). They then signal(mutex) to let other doctors in.

Exit Section: The doctor executes wait(mutex) to safely decrement readcount. If they are the very last reader leaving (readcount == 0), they execute signal(wrt), finally unlocking the database so a waiting nurse can update it.

title: Five philosophers sit at a round table with five forks between them; deadlock occurs when all five pick up their left fork at the same time. Explain this deadlock scenario in detail, and describe any two solutions discussed in class (limiting participants, all-or-nothing approach, asymmetric solution) to prevent it.
chunks:
Deadlock Scenario: If all 5 philosophers execute wait(left_fork) simultaneously, they all grab one fork. When they execute wait(right_fork), they find it's already held by their neighbour. They all wait infinitely for a right fork that will never be released (Circular Wait).

Solutions:

Limiting Participants: Allow at most 4 philosophers to sit at the 5-seat table. This guarantees at least one philosopher will have access to two forks, break the cycle, finish eating, and release their forks.

Asymmetric Solution: Number the philosophers. Even-numbered philosophers must pick up their left fork first, while odd-numbered philosophers must pick up their right fork first. This breaks the circular wait condition.

title: Critically analyze why Peterson's Solution and the Test-and-Set Lock, though correct in theory, are considered insufficient for modern operating systems, and explain how Semaphores and Monitors provide a more practical and scalable synchronization mechanism, referencing the classical synchronization problems (Bounded Buffer, Readers–Writers, Dining Philosophers) as supporting evidence.
chunks:
Why Peterson's / Test-and-Set are insufficient:

Busy Waiting: They rely on while(true) spin-loops. This wastes massive amounts of CPU cycles just checking a lock, which is catastrophic in modern multitasking systems.

Scalability: Peterson's solution mathematically only works for exactly two processes. Scaling it to 100 processes is incredibly complex.

Why Semaphores / Monitors are better:

Semaphores and Monitors use Blocking Queues instead of busy waiting. If a process cannot enter, the OS puts it to sleep (Waiting State) and switches the CPU to useful work. 

In the Bounded Buffer problem, counting semaphores trivially manage $N$ slots of data without spin-loops. In the Readers-Writers problem, semaphores scale effortlessly to allow 100 readers simultaneously. Monitors take this a step further by removing manual wait/signal logic entirely, preventing the catastrophic deadlocks commonly seen if a developer makes a mistake coding the Dining Philosophers problem.
